Secured Energy Trading Using Byzantine-Based Blockchain Consensus

Generated on: 2026-06-10 13:53:08

Executive Summary: This document serves as a self-contained, interactive HTML-PDF report detailing the benchmarking, parameter tuning, and evaluation of 5 distinct Byzantine Fault Tolerant (BFT) algorithms in the context of an IEEE 33-Bus EV-to-Grid energy trading system.

1. Simulation Environment & Parameters

To rigorously evaluate the algorithms, we designed a Python-based simulation engine (`ev_model.py` and `benchmark.py`). We did not rely on theoretical formulas alone; instead, we ran 4,250 empirical simulation trials. The parameters for the simulation were defined as follows:

  • Network Model: IEEE 33-bus radial distribution system.
  • Node Types: 50 Electric Vehicles (EVs) acting as validator nodes, and 1 Distribution Network Operator (Grid Node). Total baseline n = 51.
  • Fault Simulation (f): Up to 16 nodes were programmed as Byzantine traitors (acting maliciously).
  • Energy Trading Constraints: Transactions were only validated if EV Battery SOC ≥ 75% and transaction size was bounded (e.g., 150 kWh limit).

2. Evaluated Algorithms

The core of this research compares five specific consensus mechanisms:

  1. Classical PBFT: The standard 3-phase commit algorithm (Pre-Prepare, Prepare, Commit). Highly secure but extremely message-heavy ($O(n^2)$).
  2. Oral Messages OM(m): The theoretical baseline from Lamport's original 1982 paper. Uses recursive querying ($O(n^m)$).
  3. DAG-BFT (Hashgraph): Uses "Gossip-about-Gossip" and virtual voting, removing the need for heavy explicit network votes.
  4. Sharding-BFT: Partitions the network into smaller subsets to process transactions in parallel to increase speed.
  5. Tower BFT: A sequential, time-based protocol leveraging Proof of History (PoH) as a cryptographic clock to order events before consensus.

3. Overall Comparison & Results

A. Latency & Scalability

We swept the network size from $n=10$ to $n=500$. Classical PBFT and OM(m) degrade exponentially due to their communication overhead. Tower BFT and DAG-BFT maintain a much flatter, scalable curve. OM(m) was capped at $n=50$ due to memory overflow.

Figure 1: Consensus Latency vs. Network Size. Note the logarithmic scale.

B. Security & Byzantine Fault Tolerance

We tested the success rate of the network as the number of malicious traitors increased. The mathematical limit for BFT is $f \le \lfloor (n-1)/3 floor$, which equals 16 for our 51-node network. PBFT, Tower, and DAG maintained perfect 100% security up to exactly 16 traitors. Sharding-BFT failed early (dropping to 62% at just 10 traitors) because attackers only needed to compromise a single small shard to halt consensus.

Figure 2: Consensus Success Rate vs Fault Level. The green zone represents the theoretical safe zone.

C. Message Complexity & Overhead

The bottleneck in IoT energy grids is bandwidth. The chart below illustrates how many messages are broadcast. PBFT generates thousands of messages, while Tower BFT drastically reduces this overhead.

Figure 3: Total messages broadcast per consensus round.

4. Multi-Dimensional Verdict

The radar chart maps the algorithms across five dimensions: Latency (speed), Throughput (TPS), Message Efficiency (low bandwidth), Fault Tolerance (security), and Agreement Rate.

Figure 4: Multi-dimensional Algorithm Radar Comparison.

Conclusion

  • Tower BFT emerged as the optimal solution for EV-to-Grid networks, offering the highest throughput (996 TPS at n=51) and lowest latency (50ms) while maintaining maximum theoretical Byzantine security.
  • DAG-BFT is the runner-up, providing excellent scalability for massive networks (n > 200).
  • Sharding-BFT provides speed but introduces fatal security vulnerabilities in adversarial P2P networks.
  • Classical PBFT is secure but its $O(n^2)$ communication renders it unsuitable for large-scale decentralized EV grids.
